> 大有。元亨。

The fourteenth hexagram is named after ownership, and the character has one of the oddest entries in the dictionary.

## 有 is a hand holding meat

The form is 又 (a hand) holding 肉 (meat): to hold, to possess, to obtain.

But 說文 glosses 有 differently: 有，不宜有也。《春秋傳》曰：日月有食之 — "there is, when there should not be." The gloss is built on eclipses: a darkening that ought not to exist, and does.

That is a contested entry, and a reader of the 易 should not take it as the chapter's definition.

And 大有's 有 is heavier again. It is not "possessing an object." It is the extent of what is possessed.

The 彖: 柔得尊位，大中而上下應之，曰大有 — the yielding line holds the honored place, is great and central, and the whole body responds to it. 大有 is: what is held is great. Holding the realm.

Which makes the hexagram not about wealth but about the size of a charge.

## 亨 is read two ways in one chapter

The judgement says 元亨 — hēng, unimpeded.

九三 says 公用亨于天子 — and here 亨 is 享, xiǎng: to present, to bring tribute.

Same character, same chapter, two readings and two senses. Read it uniformly and the third line stops making sense.

This is a small technical point with a large consequence: the book keeps insisting that 不可為典要 is not a slogan. A glossary is exactly what the text defeats.

## 大車以載

大車 is the heavy cart, the ox-drawn freight wagon of the odes.

九二 大車以載，有攸往，無咎.

The image is not strength but capacity: a cart that can carry what is gathered. The line is about a person whose scale can hold what is coming to them.

Which is the hexagram's real question. 大有 is not a compliment. It is a load.

## 匪其彭

彭: 說文 彭，鼓聲也 — the sound of a drum, thence the great, the many.

九四 匪其彭，無咎 — not making it great, not displaying the abundance.

Wang Bi and 孔疏 read 彭 as 旁, "not siding with those beside one," not forming a party. Both readings work; this book takes "the great and many," because it fits the chapter's single concern: what to do with having a lot.

## 厥孚交如，威如

六五 厥孚交如，威如，吉.

孚 runs between above and below — trust circulating, each meeting the other in good faith.

威如: having gravity. Not severity, not pressure — self-respect with a boundary, so that no one treats the position lightly.

So the fifth line holds trust and weight at the same time. Which is rare enough that the text names it as the good case.

## 自天佑之，吉无不利

The top line: 自天佑之.

Not that heaven favors this person. It is that the conduct follows the order of things, and so the order holds it.

The 系辭 returns to this line and explains it at length — which is worth noticing, because it is the one place the book is most explicit that 佑 is not a gift but a fit.

## The test

Take the largest thing you currently hold — a budget, a team, a public position. Ask two questions, in this order: can the cart carry it, and are you making it great. The hexagram puts the second question after the fourth line, not the first — meaning it only becomes urgent once the capacity is established.
